newsitem.title: USA: Bennett execs indicted in largest Ponzi scheme.
newsitem.headline: Bennett execs indicted in largest Ponzi scheme.

text.p: Two members of a prominent Syracuse, N.Y., family were indicted Thursday for cheating 12,000 investors, many of them elderly, and 200 banks in what prosecutors said was the largest Ponzi scheme in history.

Bennett Funding Group Chief Financial Officer Patrick Bennett and his brother Michael, deputy chief executive, were named in a 43-count indictment alleging security and bankruptcy fraud, obstruction of justice, perjury and money laundering.
The socially prominent family is known for its contributions to charities and cultural organizations. The family's holdings include gambling casinos, a historic hotel and a race track.

Federal authorities said the defendants used the Syracuse-based Bennett Funding Group to run the largest Ponzi scheme in history and that many elderly investors lost their life savings because of the frauds.
In a Ponzi scheme, payments to early investors come from funds from later investors, not from a company's profits.
Prosecutors said the massive nationwide securities fraud resulted in the losses to investors of over $700 million in 46 states.
Bennett Funding Group leases office equipment to government agencies. From 1990 through March 1996, it acquired and sold to investors more than $2 billion in lease contracts.

It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection last year after being named in a civil suit brought by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Patrick Bennett was also named in lesser criminal charges last year.

"From beginning to end these defendants are charged with committing every variety of crime to carry out their frauds, to hide their frauds from regulators and investors and even after the scheme was unraveling and after bankruptcy was filed they tried to conceal...from creditors and investors what remaining assets there were," Manhattan U.S. Attorney Mary Jo White told a news conference.

If convicted Patrick Bennett, who was alleged mastermind of the scheme, faces up to 100 years in prison. He is the son of the company's founder. His brother faces a possible maximum of 15 years in prison.

The indictment alleged that from at least 1990 through March 1996, Patrick Bennett orchestrated the fraudulent sale to investors and pledge to banks of hundreds of millions of dollars of office equipment lease contracts.
The indictment also alleges that Patrick Bennett was engaged in a series of sham financial transactions designed to overstate the company's net income on financial statements.

Bennett Funding Group then allegedly used those financial statements in connection with the sale of notes to investors and to defraud banks and other financial institutions from which it obtained loans.
